To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neural representations of mechanical systems progress from a visual representation to an animation-based representation to a causal representation to an action representation.

(1) the neural representations of mechanical systems progress through four distinct states; (2) these states are associated with distinct patterns of brain activation; (3) these states correspond to distinct phases of instruction; (4) these states are suggestive of distinct stages of understanding; (5) the progression of these states suggests a theory of learning of simple physical systems; and (6) the theory of learning is consistent with cognitive learning theories.
neural representations of physical systems change as a person progresses through the stages of understanding the systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how people learn the workings of simple physical systems, and we suggest that neural representations can be used to understand how people progress through stages of learning, from visual encoding to mental animation to causal reasoning to action planning, and to identify the neural regions associated with these stages.
how people learn to think about physical systems, and we are developing a neural theory of learning of mechanical systems.
the neural basis of the representation and understanding of simple mechanical systems, and how that understanding changes during successive stages of incremental learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural representation of the four mechanical systems progressed through a series of four states, each of which was characterized by a unique set of brain activation patterns.
the brain representations of mechanical systems are dynamic and change as knowledge of the system changes.
the progression of representational stages was suggestive of progressive learning stages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neural representations of physical systems progress through four stages of learning: encoding information, mental animation, generating hypotheses, and interaction.
we can use neural data to track the learning of physical systems and that the neural data suggest a progression from visual encoding to causal hypotheses to motor interactions.

the neural representation of a system changes through successive stages of learning, from a predominantly visual representation (encoding the appearance of the system components) to a representation that includes parietal, frontal and motor regions (encoding mental animation, generation of hypotheses about the system, and the person's own interaction with the system).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural representation of a system changes as the learner acquires knowledge of the system.
the neural representation of a physical system changes in a progressive manner during successive stages of knowledge acquisition.
neural representations change during learning, and that these changes can be detected and quantified using a variety of neuroimaging techniques.
